1: Practical five and six. From files to numbers: image pixel distribution and audio waveform plotting. This is a hands on notebook with a sample image and a sample audio clip.
2: Unstructured files are still just numbers. Once you load them, an image or an audio clip behaves like any other numeric dataset. An image is a grid of pixels: height times width times channels. Each pixel has three numbers, red, green and blue, each from zero to two fifty five. The values are discrete and ratio scale, and the shape is structured, because every image is a fixed array. An audio clip is a list of amplitude samples over time, measured at a fixed sample rate, for example twenty two thousand fifty hertz. It is a time series, so order and spacing matter. It is a continuous signal, stored as discrete samples.
3: Practical five: image pixel distribution. Step one: load the file and look at its shape before plotting anything. The sample image is four hundred by three hundred pixels, in R G B mode with three channels. The array shape is three hundred, four hundred, three, with a value range of zero to two fifty five per channel. The code is img array equals numpy array of Image dot open of the path, and then img array dot shape.
4: Practical five: reading the pixel histogram. Step two: flatten each colour channel and count how many pixels fall at each intensity. How to read it: each tall spike is one flat coloured region in the scene, like sky, ground, sun or mountain. A natural photo usually gives a smoother, more spread out histogram, because real lighting varies pixel to pixel. The code converts the image to grey scale with convert L, and plots a histogram of the flattened grey values with fifty bins.
5: Practical six: audio waveform plotting. Step one: load the wave file. Each sample is one amplitude reading at a moment in time. The sample rate is twenty two thousand fifty hertz, the duration is two seconds, so the total is forty four thousand one hundred samples, stored as sixteen bit integers. The code reads the file with wavfile read, builds the time axis as the sample index divided by the sample rate, and plots amplitude against time. The shape you see is a plucked envelope: a quick rise and a slow fade.
6: Practical six: the waveform is a time series too. Step two: average the amplitude in small time windows to see the same trend the eye picks up. It is the same idea with familiar tools. Bucket the samples into one hundred millisecond windows and average the absolute amplitude in each, exactly like a rolling average on any other time series. This is the same trend concept from time series data, just applied to sound instead of monthly sales.
7: Recap: two new data shapes, same old toolkit. Load the file: for an image use PIL image open, and for audio use scipy wavfile read. Turn it into numbers: for an image, numpy array gives height, width and three; for audio, a one dimensional array of samples. Check its shape and range: for an image, shape, dtype, min and max; for audio, sample rate and duration. Plot the distribution: for an image, a histogram per channel; for audio, amplitude versus time. Look for structure: in an image, peaks are flat colour regions; in audio, the envelope shows loudness over time.
